title: Mastery Challenge: Psychology
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Psychology Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: One question from each chapter, from the first psychology lab to the replication crisis: what we notice, learn, remember, feel and judge. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Psychology Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the tree, from the first psychology lab to the replication crisis. Level 1 asked how you study a mind nobody can see. Now show how far you've come. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Psychology: mastered
learned: How psychology tests ideas about an unseen mind, from Wundt's lab to the replication crisis.
How perception, learning and memory filter, shape and rebuild what you experience and do.
Why mental shortcuts, other people and the way you judge events steer what you feel and decide.
How minds change across a life, and how to talk about mental health without stigma.

questions.prompt: Put these moments from across psychology in order, from earliest to latest.
items: Wundt opens the first psychology lab
questions.explanation: Wundt opened the first psychology lab in 1879, Watson launched behaviorism in 1913, Cherry named the cocktail-party problem in 1953, the invisible gorilla came in 1999, and the Open Science Collaboration reran 100 studies in 2015.

questions.prompt: A cashier busy counting a stack of bills fails to notice a customer who walks up in plain view. Which idea from Perception and Attention fits best?

options.label: The McGurk effect
options.rationale: That's sight and sound merging when you hear speech.

options.label: Weber's law
options.rationale: That's about the smallest change in a stimulus you can notice.

options.label: Inattentional blindness
Subliminal perception of ads
options.rationale: The customer was in plain view, not hidden below awareness.

questions.explanation: Attention locked on one task can hide something completely visible, like the gorilla in the 1999 basketball study.

questions.prompt: Sunglasses stop the glare that hurts your eyes, so you start reaching for them sooner. In Learning and Habits terms, this is _____.

options.label: positive punishment
options.rationale: Nothing unpleasant is added, and the behavior goes up, not down.

options.label: negative reinforcement
negative punishment
options.rationale: Punishment makes a behavior less likely; here it grows.

options.label: classical conditioning
options.rationale: Your action brings a consequence, which is operant learning.

questions.explanation: Something unpleasant is taken away (negative) and the behavior increases (reinforcement), like the seatbelt beep that stops when you buckle up.

questions.prompt: Ana rereads her notes in one long session the night before a test. Ben quizzes himself in short sessions across the week. Who likely remembers more a week later?

options.label: Ana, because rereading builds the most confidence
options.rationale: Restudiers felt surer but remembered less days later.

options.label: Both the same, since total study time is what counts
options.rationale: How you study matters, not just how long.

options.label: Ana, because one long session keeps it fresh for many weeks
options.rationale: Spaced sessions beat cramming for lasting memory.

options.label: Ben, because retrieving and spacing both strengthen memory

questions.explanation: Practice testing and distributed practice were the only techniques rated high utility: retrieval strengthens a memory, and spacing gives it time to consolidate.

questions.prompt: A planner assumes people won't care about friendship until their safety needs are met. What did Tay and Diener's study of 123 countries suggest?

options.label: Social needs mattered to wellbeing even where safety was unmet
People met their needs strictly one floor at a time, from the bottom
options.rationale: Each need mattered largely regardless of the others.

options.label: Only food and safety were linked to wellbeing
options.rationale: Meeting each need was linked to wellbeing.

options.label: Maslow's own pyramid had predicted this exact order
options.rationale: Maslow never drew a pyramid, and said his order was not rigid.

questions.explanation: Meeting each need was linked to wellbeing largely regardless of the others; Maslow himself wrote that his order was "not nearly as rigid" as it sounded.

questions.prompt: After weeks of news coverage of shark attacks, many beachgoers feel attacks are common. Which finding from Mental Shortcuts explains the feeling?

options.label: Anchoring: the first number you hear sets the estimate
options.rationale: No number was offered; vivid cases were.

options.label: The halo effect: one good trait colors the whole person
options.rationale: That's about judging people, not risks.

options.label: Availability: vivid cases come to mind easily and feel common
Hindsight bias: outcomes seem obvious once you already know them
options.rationale: That's about rewriting past predictions.

questions.explanation: The availability heuristic judges how common something is by how easily examples come to mind, so dramatic, heavily reported risks feel bigger.

questions.prompt: A 3-year-old sees a friend leave, then watches Mom move the friend's toy from a box to a drawer. Asked where the friend will look, the child points to the drawer. What does that suggest?

options.label: The child has passed the false-belief test early
options.rationale: Pointing to the drawer is the classic wrong answer.

options.label: The child doesn't yet grasp that others can hold false beliefs
The child has simply forgotten where the toy was hidden at first
options.rationale: The question is about the friend's belief, not the child's memory.

options.label: Children in most cultures pass this test by age 2
options.rationale: Across five cultures, children passed at about age 5.

questions.explanation: Theory of mind usually develops between about 3 and 5; before then, children often answer as if others know what they know.

questions.prompt: A new coworker says little in her first meeting, and you decide she's just shy. You never weigh that it's her first day among strangers. What is this?

options.label: Festinger's cognitive dissonance
options.rationale: That's changing an attitude to fit your own actions.

options.label: The fundamental attribution error
Favoring your own in-group
options.rationale: That's preferring your group over others.

options.label: The bystander effect
options.rationale: That's about helping less when others are around.

questions.explanation: The fundamental attribution error explains other people's behavior by their traits while underestimating the situation they're in.

questions.prompt: The 1964 stressful-film study and Schachter and Singer's 1962 epinephrine study point to the same lesson. Which is it?

options.label: How you interpret what's happening shapes what you feel
The body's reaction alone fixes the emotion you feel
options.rationale: In both, the reading of the situation changed the result.

options.label: Stressful films raise stress no matter how they're framed
options.rationale: Calmer soundtracks lowered bodily stress.

options.label: Emotions can't be studied in a laboratory
options.rationale: Both were lab experiments.

questions.explanation: A calmer soundtrack lowered bodily stress, and unexplained arousal took its label from the room: the interpretation steers the feeling.

questions.prompt: From the habit of publishing results to the 2015 replication project: what makes a psychology finding trustworthy?

options.label: One striking result in a top journal
options.rationale: Many such results failed on a rerun.

options.label: A famous talk that millions of people have watched
options.rationale: Power posing had that, and still faded.

options.label: How confident the original author is
options.rationale: Confidence isn't evidence.

options.label: Other researchers repeat it and find it again

questions.explanation: Psychologists publish so others can repeat their work; findings that replicate earn trust, and many famous ones didn't.
